claims.text: Pico says he was moved to examine the secrets of the book of Moses by emulation of Lorenzo's own studies, and dedicates the work to Lorenzo.

quotes.text: Emulation of your studies, Lorenzo dei Medici, has moved me to examine the secrets of the book of Moses
These labors of mine, such as they are, the first efforts of my youth thus far, are offered to you, most illustrious Lorenzo

bears_on.note: Pico presents the Heptaplus as a gift to Lorenzo, whose leisure at Fiesole made it possible.

claims.text: Pico says the work was written at Fiesole in a retreat Lorenzo provided, made pleasanter by the constant visits of Angelo Poliziano.

quotes.text: because you provided me with the leisure of this very retreat at Fiesole in which they were born, a retreat frequently made more enjoyable by the visits, or rather the constant attendance, of your friend Angelo Poliziano

bears_on.note: Poliziano is described as a constant visitor during the writing of the Heptaplus.
Lorenzo supplied the retreat at Fiesole.

claims.text: Pico believes that the secrets of all nature are contained in the works of the six days.

quotes.text: those celebrated works of the six days, in which there is great reason for us to believe that the secrets of all nature are contained

claims.text: Pico argues that the sages of old either did not write on religious subjects or wrote of them under another guise, which is why such subjects are called mysteries.

quotes.text: it was a well-known practice of the sages of old either simply not to write on religious subjects or to write of them under some other guise. For this reason these subjects are called mysteries

judged.justification: Grounds the reading of the surface of Moses as a veil for a hidden philosophy.

claims.text: Pico says Plato himself concealed his doctrines beneath allegory, myth, mathematical images and unintelligible signs.

quotes.text: Plato himself concealed his doctrines beneath coverings of allegory, veils of myth, mathematical images, and unintelligible signs of fugitive meaning.

claims.text: Pico cites Dionysius the Areopagite, whom he calls Paul's disciple, as witness that the churches kept the more secret doctrines for oral communication to the initiated.

quotes.text: Paul's disciple Dionysius the Areopagite writes that it was a settled and holy custom in the churches not to communicate the more secret doctrines in writing but only by voice and to those who had been properly initiated.

judged.justification: Shows Pico treating Dionysius as a disciple of Paul who reports apostolic esoteric practice, the stance he takes in the Third Exposition.

claims.text: Pico holds that if Moses treats anywhere of the whole world, he does so above all where he treats of the emanation of all things from God and of the grade, number and order of the parts of the world.

quotes.text: if in any part of his work he buried the treasures of all true philosophy as in a field, he must have done so most of all in the part where avowedly and most loftily he philosophizes on the emanation of all things from God, and on the grade, number, and order of the parts of the world.

claims.text: Pico says he will pass over the Fathers, the Greek writers and the Chaldean and Hebrew interpreters, and will offer seven interpretations of his own discovery.

quotes.text: We shall make no mention at present of what Ionethes or Anchelos or the venerable Simeon bequeathed in the Chaldean language
Going beyond all these, we shall suggest seven other interpretations of our own discovery and development

open_questions.text: The proem defers any use of the Hebrew authorities; how far the Heptaplus later draws on them is left for the reader to check against the text.

judged.justification: Pico says he sets aside the Chaldean and Hebrew commentators and claims the seven interpretations as his own invention.

claims.text: Pico names three difficulties: keeping Moses from seeming to speak inadequately, keeping a single coherent line of interpretation, and avoiding making Moses say anything alien to nature or to the truths of the better philosophers.

quotes.text: The first is to keep Moses from seeming to have spoken inadequately or with too little learning and wisdom.
The second difficulty is to work out a self-consistent and coherent course of interpretation

The third difficulty is to avoid making the Prophet, or the Holy Spirit through the Prophet, assert anything strange or wonderful or alien to the nature of things as they are observed, or to the truths ascertained by the better philosophers

claims.text: Pico says he will interpret the whole creation continuously and without confusion in seven senses, and not merely one, in a completely new work.

quotes.text: See how great a task we have conceived, which it may not be easy to carry out (May we be able to achieve it!), to interpret the entire creation of the world continuously and without confusion in not merely one but seven senses, without reference to earlier works, but producing a work completely new from the beginning!

claims.text: The translators' note identifies Simeon, named by Pico among the authors in the Chaldean language, as the reputed author of the Zohar.

quotes.text: Simeon ben Yohai. reputed 2nd-century author of the most important of all Cabalistic works. the Zohar, a mystical commentary on the Pentateuch.
